In 2017 an excavation at Fenstanton in Cambridgeshire found a man who died between AD 130 and 360 with a 5 cm iron nail driven horizontally through his right heel bone. He was laid out in the settlement cemetery like the others. The Cambridge team calls skeletal evidence of crucifixion extremely rare.
Skeptic: Both real victims had a nail through the side of the heel, while the Shroud shows a puncture near the middle of the sole of the right foot. With only two skeletons, crucifixion clearly varied, so the Shroud's wounds cannot be matched to Roman practice in detail. The burials show only that a crucified man could be buried properly, which fits the Gospels, not this cloth in particular.
Reply: That is fair, and the finds cut both ways. They correct the popular claim that crucified men were always thrown into mass graves, so a proper burial in a linen sheet is historically possible. And if methods varied, a nail through the sole is not ruled out either. These finds are context for the debate, not evidence for or against the cloth.
Sources: Biblical Archaeology Review on Zias and Sekeles 1985, Israel Exploration Journal 35(1):22-27 https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/department/scholars-corner-new-analysis-of-the-crucified-man; Biblical Archaeology Society, Roman crucifixion methods https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/biblical-topics/crucifixion/roman-crucifixion-methods-reveal-the-history-of-crucifixion/; Wikipedia: Jehohanan https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehohanan; University of Cambridge 2021, Evidence of a Roman crucifixion found in Cambridgeshire https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/romancrucifixion

### Under ultraviolet light the image does not glow, but the scorches do (argument for authenticity, rated moderate)
Ultraviolet photographs from 1978 show that the body image does not fluoresce while the 1532 scorches do, which argues against a scorch, and that many blood marks have a lighter border that the authors read as blood serum.
Vernon Miller and Samuel Pellicori photographed the whole cloth under ultraviolet light during the 1978 examination and published the results in the Journal of Biological Photography in 1981. They write that 'scorches emit a reddish brown fluorescence while the body image is nonfluorescent,' and conclude that 'hypotheses such as a scorch cause or paint are contradicted by the fluorescence photography results.' The blood areas absorb ultraviolet, as whole blood did in their lab tests. They also describe 'the lighter bordering area seen with many bloodstained areas,' including fluorescing borders at the hand and foot wounds, and offer the interpretation that 'blood serum is present.' The borders were photographed, not tested chemically.
Skeptic: A pale edge around a stain is what you get whenever a water-based liquid soaks into cloth: the water spreads further than the coloured part and leaves a lighter tide line. That shows a liquid soaked in, not that serum separated from a real clot. As for the image, not fluorescing rules out a high-heat scorch like the 1532 burns, but it says nothing about how or when the image was made. ENEA's laser colouring of linen, for example, is also non-fluorescent.
Reply: The scorch result is the strongest part and it holds: the image does not behave like the scorches on the same cloth. The serum reading is an interpretation, but it fits STURP's report that the blood areas test positive for serum albumin. Both points would be stronger with modern imaging and targeted sampling of the borders.
Sources: Miller and Pellicori 1981, Journal of Biological Photography 49(3):71-85 https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/UV%20Fluorescence%20Miller%20Pellicori%201981%20OCRsm.pdf; STURP 1981 summary of conclusions https://www.shroud.com/78conclu.htm

### X-rays show the weave but no body image (argument for authenticity, rated moderate)
X-ray radiographs taken in 1978 show the weave, patches and water-stain edges, but no trace of the body image, which rules out a dense layer of paint or pigment.
Mottern, London and Morris X-rayed the cloth in 1978 and reported in Materials Evaluation that 'details of the two body images, the blood stains and the scorch marks are not discernible in the radiographs,' while the herringbone weave, the backing cloth, the patches and ring-like dense areas matching the water stains do show. Schwalbe and Rogers (1982) sum up: 'No density discontinuities that correspond to visible body image could be observed anywhere,' although the weave and cloth density variations 'are easily visible in all of the radiographs.'
Skeptic: Radiography is a blunt tool for this question. Schwalbe and Rogers themselves say its sensitivity to iron oxide and similar pigments is roughly ten times lower than that of X-ray fluorescence. The radiographs do not show the blood marks either, which contain iron, so they would not show a thin, watery wash of ochre of the kind McCrone described. They rule out a heavy painted layer, not a dilute one.
Reply: Correct, and the claim should stay that narrow. The more sensitive tests point the same way: STURP's summary says X-ray fluorescence and microchemistry on the fibrils 'preclude the possibility of paint' as the source of the image. The radiographs add one independent line of evidence that no thick pigment layer is present.
Sources: Mottern, London and Morris, Materials Evaluation 38(12):39-44 https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/Radiographic%20Examination%20Preliminary%20Report%20Mottern%20London%20Morris%201979%20OCRsm.pdf; Schwalbe and Rogers 1982, Analytica Chimica Acta 135:3-49 https://shroud.com/pdfs/Physics%20Chemistry%20of%20Shroud%20Schwalbe%20Rogers%201981%20OCRsm.pdf; STURP 1981 summary of conclusions https://www.shroud.com/78conclu.htm

### Early icons of Christ share details with the Shroud face (argument for authenticity, rated disputed)
Supporters argue that the standard face of Christ in Byzantine art, from about the 6th century, copies odd details of the Shroud face, so the cloth must have existed and been seen by then.
In the late 1930s Paul Vignon listed unusual features shared by many icons and the Shroud face, such as a square-shaped mark between the brows; they became known as the Vignon markings. Alan and Mary Whanger later developed a way to compare two faces by projecting them through polarizing filters, published in Applied Optics in 1985. That paper describes the method only; their results come from later conference papers. There they report about 250 'points of congruence' between the Shroud face and the 6th-century Christ Pantocrator icon at St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, and 145 with a gold coin of Justinian II (AD 692-695), against a threshold of 45 to 60 that they take from forensic face matching.
Skeptic: The link can run the other way. A 14th-century maker would naturally copy the face of Christ that Byzantine art had used for some 800 years, so a match is expected from a forgery too. The markings are picked out after the fact on faint, blotchy features. Hugh Farey, reading Vignon's own text, shows that the popular list includes marks Vignon never named, and that Vignon treated almost any resemblance as proof of copying while explaining away the differences. Points of congruence are counted by the researchers who propose the link, and forensic thresholds were never designed for paintings.
Reply: The direction of copying is a real problem, and overlays cannot settle it. The narrower point supporters can make is that the Sinai icon and the Justinian II coins are dated centuries before 1350, so if any detail on them could only come from the Shroud, the cloth would be older than its carbon date. So far that case rests on the judgment of the people doing the matching.
Sources: Whanger and Whanger 1985, Applied Optics 24(6):766-772 https://doi.org/10.1364/AO.24.000766; M. Whanger 2000, The Impact of the Shroud Face on Art Work, Sindone 2000 congress https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/orvWHANGER%20M.%20Paper%20English.PDF; Farey 2019, The Vignon Markings, according to Paul Vignon himself https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/anc-farey-pap2.pdf

### In 1201 the palace burial linens were described with no image (argument against authenticity, rated moderate)
Skeptics argue: the keeper of the imperial relics in Constantinople described Jesus' burial linens in 1201 as plain, inexpensive linen that smelled of myrrh, with no image, which makes it unlikely that a cloth with a full-body image was there.
During the failed palace revolt of John Comnenus in 1201 (some scholars date it to 1200), Nicholas Mesarites, custodian of the holy things in the churches of the Grand Palace, defended the relic church of the Virgin of the Pharos. His account of the revolt includes a list of its relics: 'The burial shrouds of Jesus; these are of linen, an inexpensive fabric, which still smell of myrrh.' He says nothing about an image on them. In the same list he does describe an image of Christ 'imprinted on a towel,' a separate relic. The Greek text was edited by August Heisenberg in 1907; an English excerpt appeared in Shroud Spectrum International in 1985.
Skeptic: This is an eyewitness who looked after these relics, writing in the same list where he took care to note an image on a towel. If the linens had borne a full-length figure of the crucified Christ, that would have been the most striking thing about them. His plain linens also weaken Robert de Clari's report, two or three years later, of a shroud in the city showing the figure of the Lord.
Reply: Mesarites was writing a rhetorical speech, a list he calls a decalogue of relics with a sentence or two for each, not a description of each object, so his silence about an image is weak evidence. He uses the plural, 'burial shrouds,' and may mean several cloths. The passage does show that linens venerated as Jesus' burial cloths were kept in the palace in 1201, which the Edessa and de Clari hypotheses need. It cannot show whether one of them was this Shroud.
Sources: Mesarites, The Palace Revolution of John Comnenus (excerpts), Shroud Spectrum International 17, 1985 https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/ssi17part4.pdf; Wikipedia: John Komnenos the Fat https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Komnenos_the_Fat

## Claims you will hear, checked

### "The carbon dating has been debunked." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: overstated)
The 1988 test has real weak points. All samples came from one corner, and when the raw data were released, reanalyses found the measurements do not agree with each other as well as the published result implied. But no laboratory has produced a new date, and no reanalysis has moved the result to the first century. Criticizing a test is not the same as overturning it. The 1988 date is still the strongest evidence against authenticity.

### "The samples were switched, or the result was rigged." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: no evidence)
Some writers accused the laboratories or the organizers of swapping the Shroud samples for medieval cloth. No evidence of a swap has ever been produced. The cutting was filmed and witnessed, and each laboratory also dated control cloths of known age and got those dates right.
Sources: Damon et al. 1989, Nature 337:611 https://doi.org/10.1038/337611a0; Wikipedia: Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud of Turin https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating_of_the_Shroud_of_Turin

### "The labs dated an invisible medieval repair." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
Chemist Raymond Rogers reported that threads from the dated corner differ from the main cloth. Others examined a leftover piece of the 1988 sample and found no sign of a repair. Possible, not shown.

### "The 1532 fire, bacteria or a burst of neutrons changed the date." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: no evidence)
Each idea has been proposed and none has been shown. To make a first-century cloth test as medieval, a large share of the carbon in the sample, roughly a third or more, would have to be later contamination that survived the lab cleaning. No one has found it.

### "New scientific methods dated it to the time of Christ." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
Two newer methods, X-ray scattering on one thread and Fanti's fiber tests, gave results compatible with the first century. Neither method has been tested on many cloths of known age, and both depend on assumptions. Promising, not a date.

### "You can see coins over the eyes, writing and flowers in the image." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
These shapes show up only in heavily processed photographs, and other researchers looking at the same images do not see them. The human eye easily finds patterns in noise. We do not count them as evidence.

### "Pollen proves the cloth was in Jerusalem." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
The pollen came from sticky tape samples taken in the 1970s. A later pollen expert concluded the grains cannot be identified down to the plant species, so the Jerusalem conclusion should be set aside until new samples are studied. That has not happened yet.

### "The blood is type AB, the same as other famous relics." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
Typing very old, degraded blood is unreliable, and AB is a known false result with aged samples. The evidence that the stains are blood is good. The blood type is not settled.

### "The Sudarium of Oviedo confirms it." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: unproven)
The Sudarium is a face cloth kept in Oviedo, Spain. Matching its stains to the Shroud is a matter of interpretation, and radiocarbon tests on the Sudarium itself gave dates around the 7th century. It cannot add weight to the Shroud.

### "The Church has declared it authentic." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: false)
The Catholic Church has never ruled that it is authentic. In 1998 Pope John Paul II said the Church has no specific competence to decide the question and leaves it to science. Popes call it an icon. Allowing veneration is not a verdict.

### "NASA proved the image is 3D." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: overstated)
The 3D effect is real and is in the case file. But it was found in 1976 by two U.S. Air Force scientists, John Jackson and Eric Jumper, using a VP-8 Image Analyzer. It was not a NASA study, although some members of the later 1978 team worked at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The 3D effect shows the image relates to distance from a body. It does not show how the image was made.
Sources: STERA: the VP-8 discovery https://shroud.com/78strp10.htm

### "Scientists say it took 34 trillion watts of light to make the image." (usually said for authenticity; verdict: overstated)
The number comes from Italian laser experiments (ENEA, 2011) that colored small pieces of linen with ultraviolet pulses. The researchers estimated the power their method would need for a whole body image and noted no light source today can deliver it. That is an estimate about their own method. It is not a measurement taken from the Shroud, and it is not evidence of a resurrection.
Sources: Di Lazzaro et al. 2011, ENEA report RT/2011/14 (Italian) http://opac.bologna.enea.it:8991/RT/2011/2011_14_ENEA.pdf

### "Leonardo da Vinci made it." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: false)
The cloth was already on display in Lirey, France, in the 1350s, and a pilgrim badge from that time still survives. Leonardo was born in 1452, about a century later.
Sources: Lirey pilgrim badge, Musée de Cluny https://sindonology.org/papers/clunySouvenir.shtml; Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Shroud_of_Turin

### "The forger confessed in the Middle Ages." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: partly true)
A real letter from Bishop Pierre d'Arcis in 1389 says an earlier bishop found the artist who painted it. This is serious evidence and it is in the case file. But the artist is never named and no record of that earlier inquiry has been found. It is a report of a confession, not a confession we can read.

### "It is just a painting. Paint was found on it." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: partly true)
Walter McCrone found tiny paint particles and concluded it was painted. The 1978 team found that the image itself has no pigment, binder or brush marks, and that scattered particles likely came from painted copies pressed against it over the centuries. Paint particles are on the cloth. The image is not made of them.

### "Scientists have made a perfect copy." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: overstated)
Several copies come close in a photograph, the best known by Luigi Garlaschelli in 2009. Up close each one differs. In his copy the color sits in pigment, not only in the thin top layer of the fibers. Every copy so far matches some features, and none matches all of them.

### "It is a medieval photograph." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: no evidence)
Some writers proposed that someone in the Middle Ages used a camera obscura and light-sensitive chemicals, and a modern researcher made a similar image with a quartz lens and silver salts. But the 1978 X-ray fluorescence tests found no silver or other photographic chemicals in the image area, and there is no record of such technology at the time.
Sources: Morris, Schwalbe, London 1980, X-Ray Spectrometry 9(2):40-47 https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/XRay%20Fluorescence%20Morris%20Schwalbe%20London%201980%20OCRsm.pdf

### "It is a scorch from a heated statue." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: no evidence)
Scorches on linen glow under ultraviolet light. The burns from the 1532 fire on the Shroud do glow. The body image does not. That makes a simple scorch unlikely.

### "The Gospels say Jesus was wrapped in strips, not one sheet." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: partly true)
Mark, Matthew and Luke use sindon, a linen sheet. John uses othonia, a plural word for linen cloths, and mentions a separate face cloth. The words can fit one large sheet plus smaller cloths. The Gospels neither prove nor rule out the Shroud.

### "There were many 'shrouds of Jesus', so this is just one more." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: partly true)
True, medieval Europe had several cloths claimed as Jesus's burial cloths. The one at Cadouin in France turned out to be an Egyptian fabric from around 1100, with an Arabic inscription naming a caliph. But none of them carries an image like this one. Many fakes tell us to be careful. They do not tell us that this one is fake.
Sources: The Cloth of Cadouin, Shroud Spectrum International 18 https://www.shroud.com/pdfs/ssi18part5.pdf

### "The Church admitted it is a fake." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: false)
No pope or Church body has declared it a fake, just as none has declared it authentic. In 1390 a pope at Avignon allowed it to be shown only as a representation, and today popes call it an icon. Both leave the question of its origin open.

### "Jesus never existed, so it cannot be his." (usually said against authenticity; verdict: false)
Almost all historians of the period, including skeptics, agree that Jesus of Nazareth lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. The Roman historian Tacitus mentions his execution around the year 116. Whether this cloth is his is a separate question, and that question is what this site is about.
Sources: Wikipedia: Historicity of Jesus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historicity_of_Jesus; Wikipedia: Tacitus on Jesus https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacitus_on_Jesus

## Timeline
- c. AD 30 or 33: Crucifixion and burial of Jesus (hypothesized). The Gospels say Joseph of Arimathea wrapped the body in a linen cloth (sindon) and laid it in a rock tomb. John mentions linen cloths and a separate face cloth. Any link to this Shroud is a hypothesis.
- early 4th century: Eusebius records the Abgar letters, no image (legendary). Eusebius preserves a letter between King Abgar of Edessa and Jesus. No image is mentioned. The image enters the legend later.
- 384: Pilgrim Egeria sees letters, not an image (documented). Egeria visits Edessa and reports the Abgar letters but no image of Christ.
- c. 593: First mention of an Edessa image (hypothesized). Evagrius Scholasticus credits a miraculous image with saving Edessa from the Persian siege of 544. Ian Wilson later proposed this face image was the Shroud folded so only the face showed.
- 614: Sudarium said to leave Jerusalem (legendary). Legend says the face cloth now at Oviedo left Jerusalem ahead of the Persian invasion. The story is recorded centuries later by Bishop Pelagius, known as a forger.
- 944: Mandylion moved to Constantinople (hypothesized). The Image of Edessa is taken to Constantinople and placed in the Pharos chapel. The transfer is documented; that it was this Shroud is a hypothesis rejected by most historians.
- 14 March 1075: Sudarium chest opened at Oviedo (documented). Alfonso VI, his sister and El Cid open the chest holding the Sudarium. It is the earliest explicit record of that cloth.
- 1192-1195: Pray Codex drawing (hypothesized). A Hungarian manuscript shows Christ's burial with crossed hands, no thumbs, and a cloth with L-shaped circles like the Shroud's old burn holes. Critics read the object as a decorated tombstone.
- 1201: Mesarites lists plain burial linens (documented). Nicholas Mesarites, keeper of the palace relics in Constantinople, lists Jesus' burial linens as plain, inexpensive linen that still smells of myrrh. He mentions no image on them, though he describes an image of Christ on a separate towel.
- 1203-1204: Robert de Clari's figured shroud (hypothesized). A French crusader writes that a shroud showing the figure of the Lord was raised every Friday at Blachernae in Constantinople. No other source confirms it.
- 1204: Sack of Constantinople (hypothesized). Crusaders loot the city's relics. Some historians suggest a burial cloth disappeared then and later reached France. This is a hypothesis.
- 1287: Templar initiate kisses a linen image (hypothesized). Arnaut Sabbatier testified he was shown a long linen cloth with a bearded man's image at his Templar initiation. Barbara Frale proposed in 2009 that this was the Shroud.
- 20 June 1353: Lirey church founded (documented). Knight Geoffroi de Charny founds a collegiate church at Lirey in Champagne. The official Turin site calls this the start of the first certain evidence.
- c. 1355: First showings at Lirey (probable). Canon Robert de Caillac begins exhibiting the cloth at Lirey. Pilgrim badges bearing the Charny and Vergy arms, one now in the Musee de Cluny, show front and back images of a body.
- 1356: Geoffroi de Charny dies at Poitiers (documented). The founder of Lirey is killed at the Battle of Poitiers. He never left a written account of how he got the cloth.
- 1355-1382 (likely after 1370): Oresme calls a Champagne shroud a fake (documented). Theologian Nicole Oresme cites a church in Champagne claiming the Lord's shroud as a clear case of clerical fraud. The passage was identified by Nicolas Sarzeaud in 2025.
- 1389: Bishop d'Arcis memorandum (documented). The Bishop of Troyes writes to Antipope Clement VII that the cloth is cunningly painted and that an artist confessed to an earlier bishop. The surviving texts are unsigned drafts.
- 6 January 1390: Clement VII allows display as a 'representation' (documented). The antipope permits showings only if it is announced as a figure or representation, with no candles, incense or guard of honour.
- 1418: Removed from Lirey (documented). During the Hundred Years War, Marguerite de Charny takes the cloth from Lirey for safekeeping. The canons later sue for its return.
- 1453: Passes to the House of Savoy (documented). Marguerite de Charny transfers the cloth to Duke Louis of Savoy. It stays Savoy property until 1983.
- 1506: Julius II approves a feast (documented). Pope Julius II approves a liturgical feast of the Holy Shroud for Savoy on 4 May, treating it as a relic.
- 4 December 1532: Fire at Chambery (documented). Fire in the Sainte-Chapelle of Chambery melts part of the silver reliquary. Molten metal burns through the folded cloth, leaving a symmetrical pattern of holes and scorches.
- 1534: Poor Clare nuns patch the holes (documented). The nuns sew patches over the burn holes and add a Holland cloth backing.
- 1543: Calvin attacks it (documented). John Calvin's Treatise on Relics mocks the shroud shown at Nice as a fake.
- 14 September 1578: Moved to Turin (documented). Duke Emmanuel Philibert brings the cloth to Turin, the occasion being a pilgrimage by Carlo Borromeo. It has stayed in Turin since, apart from wartime removals.
- 1694: Guarini chapel and Valfre repairs (documented). The cloth is placed in Guarino Guarini's chapel, where it rests until 1993. Sebastian Valfre reinforces it.
- 1868: Princess Clotilde repairs it (documented). Clotilde of Savoy repairs the cloth. It is displayed from 24 to 27 April 1868 for the wedding of the future Umberto I.
- 28 May 1898: Secondo Pia's negative (documented). Amateur photographer Secondo Pia finds that his negative plate shows a clear, positive-looking human figure. Modern scientific interest begins here.
- 1902: Vignon studies the image geometry (documented). Paul Vignon studies how a cloth over a body would distort an image and notes the image looks like an orthogonal projection, a point raised again by Moraes in 2025.
- 1931: Enrie's photographs (documented). Professional photographer Giuseppe Enrie confirms Pia's result with sharper plates. Enrie's images were used in later 3D and 2025 modelling work.
- 1968: A crucified man's heel bone is found (documented). Builders at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem uncover a Jewish tomb with the ossuary of Yehohanan, whose right heel bone is still pierced by an iron nail. A 1985 restudy finds the nail went through one heel, from the side.
- 1969: First scientific commission (documented). The Archbishop of Turin appoints a commission, kept confidential at first, to examine the cloth's condition.
- 23 November 1973: First TV exposition and first samples (documented). The cloth is shown live on television. Threads are cut for study, including those Gilbert Raes examined, and Max Frei takes tape samples for pollen.
- 1976: VP-8 analyser shows 3D information (documented). Using a VP-8 Image Analyzer at Sandia, John Jackson and Eric Jumper find an Enrie photo gives a coherent relief. This leads to the formation of STURP.
- 26 August to October 1978: Public exposition and STURP examination (documented). About 3 million people view the cloth. Afterwards the STURP team studies it for five days around the clock, taking photos, spectra, X-ray fluorescence and sticky-tape samples.
- 1979-1990: McCrone says it is paint (documented). Walter McCrone reports red ochre and vermilion in a collagen binder on the 1978 tapes and concludes it is a 14th-century painting. He leaves STURP in 1980 and publishes his case in Accounts of Chemical Research in 1990.
- 1980: STURP papers in Applied Optics (documented). STURP publishes spectral, infrared, UV and blood results, including Heller and Adler's 'Blood on the Shroud of Turin'.
- 1981: STURP final summary (documented). STURP concludes the image is not paint and not the product of an artist, the stains contain hemoglobin, and how the image formed remains a mystery. Heller and Adler publish their chemical study.
- 1983: Given to the Holy See (documented). Ownership passes from the House of Savoy to the Holy See. A papal custodian, the Archbishop of Turin, looks after it.
- 1984: Image intensity versus distance paper (documented). Jackson, Jumper and Ercoline publish in Applied Optics that image shading correlates with cloth-to-body distance (r squared 0.60 from 13 points).
- September-October 1986: Seven labs propose a dating plan (documented). At a meeting in Turin, seven radiocarbon labs (five AMS and two small gas-counter labs) recommend a protocol for dating the cloth.
- October 1987: Only three labs are chosen (documented). Acting on instructions from the Holy See, the Archbishop of Turin selects three AMS labs: Arizona, Oxford and Zurich. The Nature paper reports that blind testing was also dropped.
- 21 April 1988: Radiocarbon sample cut (documented). In the cathedral sacristy, Giovanni Riggi cuts a strip from one corner. Pieces go to Arizona, Oxford and Zurich, with three control cloths. Part is kept in reserve.
- February 1989: Nature publishes AD 1260-1390 (documented). Damon and colleagues from the three labs report a 95% range of AD 1260-1390 and call it conclusive evidence of a medieval date. Cardinal Ballestrero announced the official range on behalf of the Church.
- 1990, 1992, 2007: Sudarium of Oviedo radiocarbon dated (documented). Arizona, Toronto and Madrid date the Sudarium to between the 6th and 9th centuries, most likely around AD 700.
- 11 April 1997: Cathedral fire (documented). Fire breaks out in the Guarini chapel. Firefighter Mario Trematore smashes the bulletproof case with a sledgehammer and the cloth is carried out unharmed.
- 24 May 1998: John Paul II: not a matter of faith (documented). In Turin, the pope says the Church has no specific competence to rule on authenticity and entrusts the question to scientists, calling the Shroud a mirror of the Gospel.
- 2000: Great Jubilee exposition (documented). The cloth is shown publicly for the Jubilee year.
- 20 June to 22 July 2002: Major restoration (documented). Mechthild Flury-Lemberg's team removes the 30 patches of 1534 and the Holland backing, fits a new backing, and scans both sides. Some scholars criticise the work as damaging evidence.
- 2004: Claimed faint image on the back (documented). Fanti and Maggiolo report a faint face image on the reverse from 2002 photographs. Direct observers in 2002 reportedly saw none.
- January 2005: Rogers: the dated sample was different (documented). Raymond Rogers argues in Thermochimica Acta that the radiocarbon area has cotton and a gum-dye coating and estimates the cloth at 1,300 to 3,000 years old from vanillin loss.
- 2008: Oxford tests the carbon monoxide idea (documented). Christopher Ramsey tests whether carbon monoxide could add young carbon to linen and finds no significant effect.
- October 2009: Garlaschelli's full-size replica (documented). Chemist Luigi Garlaschelli shows a life-size cloth made by rubbing an acidic pigment over a volunteer and a bas-relief, then baking and washing. The paper appears in 2010.
- 2010-2011: ENEA ultraviolet laser studies (documented). ENEA physicists colour linen with very short UV laser pulses and get thin, Shroud-like yellowing. They stress this does not show how the image was actually made.
- 2010: Arizona re-examines a dated fragment (documented). Freer-Waters and Jull find no dye or coating and only a few cotton fibres on a leftover Arizona fragment. The cloth is also shown publicly in 2010.
- 2013: Statistics paper and Fanti's dating book (documented). Riani and colleagues publish the spatial-trend analysis in Statistics and Computing. Fanti announces FT-IR, Raman and mechanical dates near the first century; the Archbishop of Turin says the material's origin is not certain.
- 2014: Freeman's Easter-prop theory (documented). Historian Charles Freeman argues in History Today that the cloth was a faded, once-painted prop for medieval Easter dramas.
- 2015: Exposition and first DNA survey (documented). The cloth is shown with Pope Francis's approval. Barcaccia and colleagues report plant and human DNA from many regions, adding that a medieval European origin is not excluded.
- 2017: Raw radiocarbon data released (documented). After a legal request, the British Museum releases the 1988 labs' raw data to researcher Tristan Casabianca.
- 2018: Bloodstain pattern study (documented). Borrini and Garlaschelli report in the Journal of Forensic Sciences that the blood flows imply inconsistent postures. A public exposition is held in August.
- July 2018: Trauma blood paper retracted (documented). PLOS ONE retracts a 2017 paper that claimed nanoparticles in one Shroud fibre showed severe trauma, citing insufficient data and controls. The authors objected.
- March 2019: Raw data show heterogeneity (documented). Casabianca and colleagues publish in Archaeometry that the raw data lack homogeneity and the 1988 procedure should be reconsidered, while not ruling out a medieval date.
- Holy Saturday, April 2020: Livestreamed exposition in lockdown (documented). During the COVID-19 lockdown, the archdiocese shows the cloth by television and online. Pope Francis calls it an icon of the crucified, dead and risen Lord.
- 2020: Two more statistical reanalyses (documented). Walsh and Schwalbe, and Di Lazzaro and colleagues, publish that the shroud results are heterogeneous with a spatial trend and that the medieval conclusion should be reconsidered.
- December 2021: A crucified man found in Roman Britain (documented). Archaeologists report a man buried at Fenstanton, Cambridgeshire, who died between AD 130 and 360 with an iron nail through his right heel bone. He was given a normal burial in the settlement cemetery.
- April 2022: WAXS dating of one thread (documented). De Caro and colleagues report in Heritage that one thread's cellulose ageing matches a Masada linen of AD 55-74, under assumed storage conditions.
- February 2025: Neutral review: date stands, retest needed (documented). A review in Textiles concludes the evidence against the 1989 date is not enough to overturn it, image formation is still a mystery, and a second radiocarbon test is needed.
- 28 April to 5 May 2025: Digital Shroud for the Jubilee (documented). Instead of a physical exposition, Cardinal Repole presents a life-size digital replica in a tent in Piazza Castello, Turin.
- 28 July 2025: Moraes: a low relief fits better (documented). Cicero Moraes publishes 3D draping simulations in Archaeometry suggesting a low-relief sculpture fits the image better than a body. The Turin centre CISS replies on 4 August that this is not new.
- August 2025: Oresme passage published (documented). Nicolas Sarzeaud publishes the Oresme text in the Journal of Medieval History, the earliest known written rejection of the cloth.
- February 2026: Rebuttal to Moraes in Archaeometry (documented). Casabianca, Marinelli and Piana publish a critique of Moraes's model in the same journal, citing modelling errors and ignored evidence.
- April 2026: Second Arizona fragment examined (documented). Freer-Waters and Jull publish in Heritage Science on a leftover 1988 Arizona fragment. Press reports say they found no sign of a repair or foreign material.
- 11 June 2026: Regression on the raw data (documented). Riani, Atkinson, Corbellini and Di Lazzaro publish a reanalysis of the raw data in Statistical Methods and Applications, testing all 165,888 possible subsample layouts.
- July 2026: New examination of the Sudarium (documented). EDICES and the University of Oviedo report the first non-invasive technical examination of the Sudarium since 2012.
- July 2026: DNA study of the 1978 samples (documented). Barcaccia and colleagues report in Scientific Reports that the main human DNA matches the scientist who collected the samples, plus many plant, animal and microbial traces. Two reliquary threads date to the 1534 and 1694 repairs.
- 22 July 2026: Blood and image order tested (documented). Kelly Kearse shows that blood on acid-treated linen blocks later colouring, so 'no image under blood' does not fix the order of events.
